title: Μοῦσαι καὶ Νῆες
titleEn: The Invocation and the First Ships — Iliad 2.469–568
part: The Invocation and the First Ships (2.469–568)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The Achaeans pouring onto the plain are compared to flies swarming round a farmyard in spring, and the leaders sort them as goatherds sort mixed flocks; Agamemnon stands out among them as a bull stands out in a herd, with the eyes and head of Zeus, the waist of Ares and the chest of Poseidon. The poet then calls on the Muses, who are goddesses, were present and know everything, while he has only a report: he could not name the multitude even with ten tongues and a heart of bronze, so he asks them to recall the leaders and the ships. The Catalogue begins with the contingents in order: the Boeotians (fifty ships, a hundred and twenty young men in each), the men of Aspledon and Orchomenus under the two sons of Ares, the Phocians, the Locrians under the lesser Ajax, the Abantes of Euboea under Elephenor, the Athenians under Menestheus, twelve ships from Ajax of Salamis, and the men of Argos and its neighbourhood under Diomedes, Sthenelus and Euryalus.

sentences.t:
ἠΰτε μυιάων ἁδινάων ἔθνεα πολλὰ
αἵ τε κατὰ σταθμὸν ποιμνήϊον ἠλάσκουσιν
ὥρῃ ἐν εἰαρινῇ ὅτε τε γλάγος ἄγγεα δεύει,
sentences.tr:
ēÿte muiaōn hadinaōn ethnea polla
hai te kata stathmon poimnēïon ēlaskousin
hōrēi en eiarinēi hote te glagos angea deuei,
sentences.l:
As the many tribes of flies, thronging,
that roam about the steading of the flock
in the season of spring, when the milk wets the vessels,
sentences.i: As the many swarms of thronging flies that roam about the flock’s steading in the spring season, when the milk wets the vessels,
sentences.n: The catalogue is introduced by similes, and this first one compares the Achaeans, standing on the plain, to flies. ἠΰτε ‘as, like’ opens it. μυιάων is the epic genitive plural of μυῖα ‘fly’, and ἁδινάων ‘thronging’ is the epithet the bees had at 2.87; ἔθνεα is ‘tribes’ in the literal layer and ‘swarms’ in the English, as at 2.87 and 2.459. The relative αἵ τε is feminine plural, so it looks back to μυιάων, the flies themselves, and not to the neuter ἔθνεα; ἠλάσκουσιν is ‘roam’. κατὰ σταθμὸν ποιμνήϊον is ‘about the steading of the flock’, ποιμνήϊον being an adjective ‘of a flock’. ὥρῃ ἐν εἰαρινῇ is ‘in the spring season’, εἰαρινῇ the epic form of ἐαρινῇ. γλάγος is a rare word for ‘milk’ (= γάλα), ἄγγεα are ‘vessels’, here milk-pails, and δεύει is ‘wets’. The unit stops at a comma; the main clause follows.

sentences.t:
τόσσοι ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐν πεδίῳ ἵσταντο διαρραῖσαι μεμαῶτες.
sentences.tr:
tossoi epi Trōessi karē komoōntes Achaioi
en pediōi histanto diarraisai memaōtes.
sentences.l:
so many against the Trojans the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
on the plain were taking their stand, eager to shatter.
sentences.i: so many long-haired Achaeans took their stand on the plain against the Trojans, eager to shatter them.
sentences.n: τόσσοι ‘so many’ answers the flies, and the Achaeans are the subject. κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί is the stock phrase, ‘long-haired-of-head’ in the literal layer and ‘long-haired’ in the English, with κάρη ‘head’ an accusative of respect. ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι with the dative is ‘against the Trojans’ (Τρώεσσι is the epic dative plural). ἵσταντο is the imperfect middle of ἵστημι, ‘were taking their stand’. διαρραῖσαι, the aorist infinitive of διαρραίω ‘shatter’, has no object in the Greek; the English supplies ‘them’, the Trojans. μεμαῶτες is the perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, with present sense.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ὥς τ’ αἰπόλια πλατέ’ αἰγῶν αἰπόλοι ἄνδρες
ῥεῖα διακρίνωσιν ἐπεί κε νομῷ μιγέωσιν,
ὣς τοὺς ἡγεμόνες διεκόσμεον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
ὑσμίνην δ’ ἰέναι,
sentences.tr:
tous d’ hōs t’ aipolia plate’ aigōn aipoloi andres
rheia diakrinōsin epei ke nomōi migeōsin,
hōs tous hēgemones diekosmeon entha kai entha
hysminēn d’ ienai,
sentences.l:
And them, as the broad herds of goats goatherd men
easily sort apart, when in the pasture they have mingled,
so the leaders set them in order, this way and that,
and to go into battle,
sentences.i: And as goatherds easily sort out the broad herds of goats when they have got mixed together in the pasture, so the leaders set the men in order, this way and that, to go into battle,
sentences.n: A second simile, of herdsmen sorting mixed flocks, describes the leaders’ work. The pattern is ὥς τε … ὣς τοὺς, ‘as … so …’, and τοὺς, a demonstrative, is ‘them’, the Achaeans. In the comparison αἰπόλοι ἄνδρες ‘goatherd men’ are the subject of διακρίνωσιν, the present subjunctive of διακρίνω ‘sort apart’; its object is αἰπόλια ‘herds of goats’ with πλατέ’ (elided πλατέα) ‘broad’. ῥεῖα is ‘easily’. ἐπεί κε with the subjunctive μιγέωσιν (aorist passive of μίγνυμι, uncontracted for μιγῶσιν) is ‘when they have got mixed’, and νομῷ is the dative of νομός ‘pasture’. In the main clause διεκόσμεον is the uncontracted imperfect of διακοσμέω ‘set in order’, ἡγεμόνες are ‘leaders’, and ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα is ‘this way and that’. ὑσμίνην δ’ ἰέναι is ‘and to go into battle’, an infinitive of purpose, the δέ a loose ‘and’. The unit ends at the comma in the middle of line 477.

sentences.t:
μετὰ δὲ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
ὄμματα καὶ κεφαλὴν ἴκελος Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ,
Ἄρεϊ δὲ ζώνην, στέρνον δὲ Ποσειδάωνι.
sentences.tr:
meta de kreiōn Agamemnōn
ommata kai kephalēn ikelos Dii terpikeraunōi,
Areï de zōnēn, sternon de Poseidaōni.
sentences.l:
and among them lord Agamemnon,
in eyes and head like Zeus delighting-in-the-thunderbolt,
in girdle like Ares, and in chest like Poseidon.
sentences.i: and among them was lord Agamemnon, like Zeus who delights in the thunderbolt in eyes and head, like Ares in his waist, and like Poseidon in his chest.
sentences.n: Agamemnon is likened to three gods, each for one part of him. μετὰ δὲ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων has no verb: μετά is ‘among them’, and the English supplies ‘was’. ὄμματα, κεφαλήν, ζώνην and στέρνον are accusatives of respect (‘in eyes, in head …’), and ἴκελος ‘like’ takes the datives Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ, Ἄρεϊ and Ποσειδάωνι, the last the epic uncontracted dative of Ποσειδῶν. τερπικεραύνῳ, ‘delighting-in-the-thunderbolt’, is the epithet Zeus has at 1.419. κρείων ‘lord’ is Agamemnon’s title, as at 2.369. ζώνη is the girdle, and the English says ‘waist’, the part of the body it goes round.

sentences.t:
ἠΰτε βοῦς ἀγέληφι μέγ’ ἔξοχος ἔπλετο πάντων
ταῦρος·
sentences.tr:
ēÿte bous agelēphi meg’ exochos epleto pantōn
tauros·
sentences.l:
As in the herd an ox, greatly standing out of all,
has come to be, the bull;
sentences.i: As, in a herd, the bull stands out far above all the cattle;
sentences.n: A third simile, of the bull in the herd. ἠΰτε opens it. βοῦς ‘ox’ or ‘cow’ is the general word for a head of cattle, and ταῦρος ‘bull’ stands in apposition to it, naming which one is meant; the literal layer keeps both (‘an ox … the bull’), and the English drops the apposition and reads πάντων as ‘all the cattle’. ἀγέληφι is ‘in the herd’, the old ending -φι doing the work of a dative, and ἔπλετο is the epic aorist of πέλομαι, here a general truth, ‘has come to be’ in the literal layer and ‘stands out’ in the English. ἔξοχος is ‘standing out’, μέγ’ ‘greatly’ goes with it, and πάντων is ‘of all’. The unit ends at the ano teleia after ταῦρος, in the middle of line 481.

sentences.t: ὃ γάρ τε βόεσσι μεταπρέπει ἀγρομένῃσι·
sentences.tr: ho gar te boessi metaprepei agromenēisi·
sentences.l: for he among the cows assembling is conspicuous;
sentences.i: for he is conspicuous among the cows as they gather;
sentences.n: The reason for the comparison. ὃ γάρ τε is ‘for he’, with τε marking a general truth. μεταπρέπει is ‘is conspicuous among’ and takes the dative βόεσσι, the epic dative plural of βοῦς. ἀγρομένῃσι is the feminine dative plural of the aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω ‘gather’; its feminine ending shows that the βόες here are cows.

sentences.t:
τοῖον ἄρ’ Ἀτρεΐδην θῆκε Ζεὺς ἤματι κείνῳ
ἐκπρεπέ’ ἐν πολλοῖσι καὶ ἔξοχον ἡρώεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
toion ar’ Atreïdēn thēke Zeus ēmati keinōi
ekprepe’ en polloisi kai exochon hērōessin.
sentences.l:
Such then Atreus’-son made Zeus on that day,
distinguished among many and standing out among heroes.
sentences.i: Such, then, did Zeus make the son of Atreus on that day: distinguished among many, and standing out among heroes.
sentences.n: The comparison is applied. τοῖον ‘such (a man)’ is the accusative predicate of θῆκε ‘made’, and ἐκπρεπέ’ (elided ἐκπρεπέα) ‘distinguished’ and ἔξοχον ‘standing out’ stand in the same predicate. ἐν πολλοῖσι is ‘among many’ and ἡρώεσσιν ‘among heroes’, both epic datives plural. Ἀτρεΐδην is the son of Atreus, Agamemnon, not named in the sentence. ἤματι κείνῳ is ‘on that day’ (ἦμαρ, the epic dative; κείνῳ = ἐκείνῳ), the day of the muster. ἄρ’ is ‘then’.

sentences.t: ἔσπετε νῦν μοι Μοῦσαι Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχουσαι·
sentences.tr: espete nyn moi Mousai Olympia dōmat’ echousai·
sentences.l: Tell now to me, Muses, who hold the Olympian halls;
sentences.i: Tell me now, Muses, you who hold the halls of Olympus:
sentences.n: The similes end and the poet turns to the Muses. ἔσπετε is the aorist imperative plural of ἐνέπω ‘tell’, the verb of the Odyssey’s first line (ἔννεπε); the Iliad’s first line addressed one goddess, θεά, with ἄειδε ‘sing’. μοι is ‘to me’, and Μοῦσαι, the goddesses of song, is the vocative. Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχουσαι is the feminine of the formula ‘who hold the Olympian halls’ (1.18 and 2.13 have the masculine), with ἔχουσαι the participle of ἔχω. The speaker is the poet himself, so there are no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ὑμεῖς γὰρ θεαί ἐστε πάρεστέ τε ἴστέ τε πάντα,
ἡμεῖς δὲ κλέος οἶον ἀκούομεν οὐδέ τι ἴδμεν·
sentences.tr:
hymeis gar theai este pareste te iste te panta,
hēmeis de kleos oion akouomen oude ti idmen·
sentences.l:
For you are goddesses, and are present, and know all things,
but we hear a report alone, and know nothing;
sentences.i: For you are goddesses, you are present, and you know everything, while we hear only a report and know nothing ourselves;
sentences.n: The poet gives his reason for needing them. ὑμεῖς and ἡμεῖς, ‘you’ and ‘we’, are set against each other, goddesses and mortals. πάρεστε is ‘you are present’ (πάρειμι), and ἴστε is ‘you know’, the second plural of οἶδα in an older form; ἴδμεν is the first plural, ‘we know’. The two τε join πάρεστε and ἴστε, ‘you are present and you know’. κλέος is ‘report’, what is said and heard, and οἶον, the neuter accusative of οἶος ‘alone’, makes it ‘a report alone’; ἀκούομεν is ‘we hear’. οὐδέ τι is ‘and … nothing’.

sentences.t: οἵ τινες ἡγεμόνες Δαναῶν καὶ κοίρανοι ἦσαν·
sentences.tr: hoi tines hēgemones Danaōn kai koiranoi ēsan·
sentences.l: who were the leaders of the Danaans, and rulers;
sentences.i: who the leaders and rulers of the Danaans were;
sentences.n: These are the words the Muses are asked to supply. οἵ τινες is ‘who’ in an indirect question after ἔσπετε (484): οἵ is the relative and τινες makes it ‘whoever’, and ἦσαν is ‘were’. ἡγεμόνες ‘leaders’ and κοίρανοι ‘rulers’ are the two titles, and Δαναῶν, the genitive plural of Δαναοί, goes with both.

sentences.t: πληθὺν δ’ οὐκ ἂν ἐγὼ μυθήσομαι οὐδ’ ὀνομήνω,
sentences.tr: plēthyn d’ ouk an egō mythēsomai oud’ onomēnō,
sentences.l: But the multitude I could not tell, nor could I name it,
sentences.i: But the multitude I could not tell, nor name,
sentences.n: Even with the Muses’ help the poet asks only for the leaders. πληθύν ‘multitude’ comes first for contrast. οὐκ ἂν … μυθήσομαι is ‘could not tell’: ἄν with a future (or with a short-vowel subjunctive) says what is possible, and the Odyssey has the same words after πάντα μέν (4.240). μυθήσομαι is from μυθέομαι ‘tell, recount’, and ὀνομήνω is the aorist subjunctive of ὀνομαίνω ‘name’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἴ μοι δέκα μὲν γλῶσσαι, δέκα δὲ στόματ’ εἶεν,
φωνὴ δ’ ἄρρηκτος, χάλκεον δέ μοι ἦτορ ἐνείη,
εἰ μὴ Ὀλυμπιάδες Μοῦσαι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο
θυγατέρες μνησαίαθ’ ὅσοι ὑπὸ Ἴλιον ἦλθον·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ei moi deka men glōssai, deka de stomat’ eien,
phōnē d’ arrēktos, chalkeon de moi ētor eneiē,
ei mē Olympiades Mousai Dios aigiochoio
thygateres mnēsaiath’ hosoi hypo Ilion ēlthon·
sentences.l:
not even if for me ten tongues, and ten mouths there were,
and a voice unbreakable, and a heart of bronze for me were within,
unless the Olympian Muses, of aegis-bearing Zeus
the daughters, were to call to mind as many as beneath Ilium came;
sentences.i: not even if ten tongues were mine, and ten mouths, and an unbreakable voice, and a heart of bronze within me, unless the Olympian Muses, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, were to call to mind all who came to Ilium;
sentences.n: A long condition: not even with ten tongues could the poet name the host, unless the Muses were to recall it. οὐδ’ εἴ is ‘not even if’, and the optatives εἶεν and ἐνείη (from ἔνειμι ‘be in’) say what he does not have: δέκα μὲν γλῶσσαι, δέκα δὲ στόματ’ ‘ten tongues, ten mouths’, φωνὴ ἄρρηκτος ‘an unbreakable voice’ (α- ‘not’ + ῥήγνυμι ‘break’) and χάλκεον … ἦτορ ‘a heart of bronze’, χάλκεον being the uncontracted form of χαλκοῦν. The main verb, ‘I could not’, is carried over from 488. εἰ μή ‘unless’ brings in the exception: Ὀλυμπιάδες, a feminine adjective, ‘Olympian’, Μοῦσαι, the θυγατέρες ‘daughters’ of Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing Zeus’, the epithet translated as in the Odyssey. μνησαίαθ’ is the elided aorist optative middle of μιμνήσκομαι, ‘call to mind’; its object is the clause ὅσοι … ἦλθον ‘as many as came’, and ὑπὸ Ἴλιον is ‘up to the foot of Ilium’. Line 492 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of θυγατέρες is lengthened to serve as the long of the first foot, and the diphthong of ὅσοι is kept long in hiatus before ὑπό.

sentences.t: ἀρχοὺς αὖ νηῶν ἐρέω νῆάς τε προπάσας.
sentences.tr: archous au nēōn ereō nēas te propasas.
sentences.l: The commanders of the ships, in turn, I will tell, and the ships, all of them.
sentences.i: Next I will tell the commanders of the ships, and all the ships.
sentences.n: The plan of the Catalogue is stated: the commanders and the ships. ἀρχούς is ‘commanders’ (ἀρχός), and νηῶν, the epic genitive plural of ναῦς, goes with it. ἐρέω is the future of the verb meaning ‘say, tell’ (as at 1.76), and αὖ ‘in turn, next’ marks the move from the prayer to the list. νῆάς is the epic accusative plural of ναῦς; προπάσας, formed from πᾶς with the prefix πρό, is ‘all of them, every one’.

sentences.t:
Βοιωτῶν μὲν Πηνέλεως καὶ Λήϊτος ἦρχον
Ἀρκεσίλαός τε Προθοήνωρ τε Κλονίος τε,
sentences.tr:
Boiōtōn men Pēneleōs kai Lēïtos ērchon
Arkesilaos te Prothoēnōr te Klonios te,
sentences.l:
Of the Boeotians Peneleos and Leitus were leading,
and Arcesilaus, and Prothoenor, and Clonius,
sentences.i: Peneleos and Leitus led the Boeotians, together with Arcesilaus, Prothoenor and Clonius,
sentences.n: The Catalogue proper begins, and each entry follows one pattern: a people in the genitive, their leaders, the places they came from, and the number of ships. Βοιωτῶν μέν is ‘of the Boeotians’, and the μέν is answered at 511 by the οἳ δ’ of the next people. ἦρχον is the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead’, and its plural subject is all five names: Πηνέλεως (a nominative), Λήϊτος, Ἀρκεσίλαος, Προθοήνωρ and Κλονίος. The names take their usual English forms. The unit stops at the comma after the names.

sentences.t:
οἵ θ’ Ὑρίην ἐνέμοντο καὶ Αὐλίδα πετρήεσσαν
Σχοῖνόν τε Σκῶλόν τε πολύκνημόν τ’ Ἐτεωνόν,
Θέσπειαν Γραῖάν τε καὶ εὐρύχορον Μυκαλησσόν,
sentences.tr:
hoi th’ Hyriēn enemonto kai Aulida petrēessan
Schoinon te Skōlon te polyknēmon t’ Eteōnon,
Thespeian Graian te kai eurychoron Mykalēsson,
sentences.l:
and who inhabited Hyria and rocky Aulis,
and Schoenus and Scolus and many-spurred Eteonus,
Thespeia and Graea and Mycalessus, of wide dancing-grounds,
sentences.i: who inhabited Hyria and rocky Aulis, Schoenus, Scolus and many-spurred Eteonus, Thespeia, Graea and spacious Mycalessus,
sentences.n: A list of places, all accusatives after one verb. οἵ θ’ (οἵ τε) is ‘and who’, with the Boeotians as antecedent, and ἐνέμοντο is the imperfect middle of νέμω, ‘inhabited’, taking Ὑρίην, Αὐλίδα, Σχοῖνον, Σκῶλον, Ἐτεωνόν, Θέσπειαν, Γραῖαν and Μυκαλησσόν. The epithets are translated each time: πετρήεσσαν ‘rocky’ (feminine of πετρήεις), πολύκνημον ‘many-spurred’ (κνήμη is the shin, used of the foot or spur of a hill, which is the usual explanation) and εὐρύχορον, ‘of wide dancing-grounds’ in the literal layer (χορός is a dancing-place) and ‘spacious’ in the English, as in the Odyssey.

sentences.t: οἵ τ’ ἀμφ’ Ἅρμ’ ἐνέμοντο καὶ Εἰλέσιον καὶ Ἐρυθράς,
sentences.tr: hoi t’ amph’ Harm’ enemonto kai Eilesion kai Erythras,
sentences.l: and who inhabited around Harma, and Eilesion, and Erythrae,
sentences.i: and those who inhabited the country around Harma, and Eilesion and Erythrae,
sentences.n: οἵ τ’ is again ‘and who’. ἀμφὶ Ἅρμ’ (Ἅρμα, a place-name here, not the word for ‘chariot’) is ‘about Harma’, and the Greek leaves it open whether ἀμφί is meant to govern Εἰλέσιον and Ἐρυθράς as well. ἐνέμοντο is ‘inhabited’ as in 496. Ἐρυθράς is an accusative plural, ‘Erythrae’.

sentences.t:
οἵ τ’ Ἐλεῶν’ εἶχον ἠδ’ Ὕλην καὶ Πετεῶνα,
Ὠκαλέην Μεδεῶνά τ’ ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον,
Κώπας Εὔτρησίν τε πολυτρήρωνά τε Θίσβην,
sentences.tr:
hoi t’ Eleōn’ eichon ēd’ Hylēn kai Peteōna,
Ōkaleēn Medeōna t’ eÿktimenon ptoliethron,
Kōpas Eutrēsin te polytrērōna te Thisbēn,
sentences.l:
and who held Eleon and Hyle and Peteon,
Ocalea and Medeon, the well-built citadel,
Copae, and Eutresis, and Thisbe rich in doves,
sentences.i: and who held Eleon, Hyle and Peteon, Ocalea and Medeon, the well-built citadel, Copae, Eutresis, and Thisbe rich in doves,
sentences.n: The verb is now εἶχον ‘held’. Ἐλεῶν’ is the elided Ἐλεῶνα, and the objects run on through the next two lines: Ἐλεῶνα, Ὕλην, Πετεῶνα; Ὠκαλέην, Μεδεῶνα; Κώπας, Εὔτρησιν, Θίσβην. ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον ‘the well-built citadel’ is the stock epithet of a walled town, here in apposition to Medeon, and is translated as in the Odyssey. πολυτρήρωνα ‘rich in doves’ is built on πολύ- ‘many’ and τρήρων, a word applied to doves; the sense given is the usual explanation. Εὔτρησιν is the accusative singular of Εὔτρησις.

sentences.t:
οἵ τε Κορώνειαν καὶ ποιήενθ’ Ἁλίαρτον,
οἵ τε Πλάταιαν ἔχον ἠδ’ οἳ Γλισᾶντ’ ἐνέμοντο,
οἵ θ’ Ὑποθήβας εἶχον ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον,
sentences.tr:
hoi te Korōneian kai poiēenth’ Haliarton,
hoi te Plataian echon ēd’ hoi Glisant’ enemonto,
hoi th’ Hypothēbas eichon eÿktimenon ptoliethron,
sentences.l:
and who (held) Coroneia and grassy Haliartus,
and who held Plataea, and who Glisas inhabited,
and who held Hypothebae, the well-built citadel,
sentences.i: those who held Coroneia and grassy Haliartus, those who held Plataea and those who inhabited Glisas, and those who held Hypothebae, the well-built citadel,
sentences.n: Three more clauses with οἵ τε ‘and who’. In 503 there is no verb, and ‘held’ is supplied from the clauses around it; 504 has both ἔχον ‘held’ (Plataea) and ἐνέμοντο ‘inhabited’ (Glisas), and 505 has εἶχον. ποιήενθ’ is ποιήεντα, ‘grassy’ (from ποίη ‘grass’), elided before the rough breathing of Ἁλίαρτον, which turns τ into θ. Γλισᾶντ’ is the elided accusative Γλισᾶντα. ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον ‘the well-built citadel’ is now said of Hypothebae.

sentences.t:
Ὀγχηστόν θ’ ἱερὸν Ποσιδήϊον ἀγλαὸν ἄλσος,
οἵ τε πολυστάφυλον Ἄρνην ἔχον, οἵ τε Μίδειαν
Νῖσάν τε ζαθέην Ἀνθηδόνα τ’ ἐσχατόωσαν·
sentences.tr:
Onchēston th’ hieron Posidēïon aglaon alsos,
hoi te polystaphylon Arnēn echon, hoi te Mideian
Nisan te zatheēn Anthēdona t’ eschatoōsan·
sentences.i: and sacred Onchestus, Poseidon’s splendid grove, and those who held Arne, rich in grapes, and those who held Mideia, most holy Nisa, and Anthedon, lying at the edge;
sentences.n: Onchestus (Ὀγχηστόν, accusative) is ἱερόν ‘sacred’ and is glossed as Ποσιδήϊον ἀγλαὸν ἄλσος, ‘Poseidon’s splendid grove’: Ποσιδήϊον is an adjective ‘of Poseidon’, ἄλσος a ‘grove’, a sacred precinct, and ἀγλαός ‘splendid’. The verb is still ‘held’ (ἔχον in 507), for Arne with πολυστάφυλον ‘rich in grapes’ and, understood, for Mideia, Nisa and Anthedon. ζαθέην ‘most holy’ is the epithet Cilla had at 1.38. ἐσχατόωσαν is the participle of ἐσχατάω ‘lie at the edge’, with the epic -όω-, so ‘lying at the edge’, the outermost town. The unit ends at the ano teleia that closes the list of places.

sentences.t:
τῶν μὲν πεντήκοντα νέες κίον, ἐν δὲ ἑκάστῃ
κοῦροι Βοιωτῶν ἑκατὸν καὶ εἴκοσι βαῖνον.
sentences.tr:
tōn men pentēkonta nees kion, en de hekastēi
kouroi Boiōtōn hekaton kai eikosi bainon.
sentences.l:
Of these fifty ships went, and in each
young men of the Boeotians a hundred and twenty were embarking.
sentences.i: Fifty ships of theirs went, and in each of them a hundred and twenty young men of the Boeotians were embarking.
sentences.n: The entry closes with its number. τῶν μέν is ‘of these’, a genitive of belonging, and νέες is the epic nominative plural of ναῦς (Attic νῆες). κίον is the imperfect of κίω ‘go’, and βαῖνον the imperfect of βαίνω, both unaugmented; ἐν … ἑκάστῃ is ‘in each’, with ‘ship’ understood. κοῦροι is ‘young men’, and ἑκατὸν καὶ εἴκοσι is ‘a hundred and twenty’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ Ἀσπληδόνα ναῖον ἰδ’ Ὀρχομενὸν Μινύειον,
τῶν ἦρχ’ Ἀσκάλαφος καὶ Ἰάλμενος υἷες Ἄρηος
οὓς τέκεν Ἀστυόχη δόμῳ Ἄκτορος Ἀζεΐδαο,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ Asplēdona naion id’ Orchomenon Minyeion,
tōn ērch’ Askalaphos kai Ialmenos huies Arēos
hous teken Astyochē domōi Aktoros Azeïdao,
sentences.l:
And those who dwelt in Aspledon and Minyan Orchomenus,
of these were leading Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, sons of Ares,
whom Astyoche bore in the house of Actor, Azeus’-son,
sentences.i: Those who dwelt in Aspledon and Minyan Orchomenus were led by Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, sons of Ares, whom Astyoche bore in the house of Actor, son of Azeus,
sentences.n: A new people, in a new paragraph. οἳ δ’ is ‘and those who’, the δέ answering Βοιωτῶν μέν (494). Ἀσπληδόνα and Ὀρχομενὸν Μινύειον ‘Minyan Orchomenus’ (Μινύειον ‘of the Minyans’) are the objects of ναῖον, the unaugmented imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell in’ (= ἔναιον); ἰδ’ is ἠδέ ‘and’. τῶν ἦρχ’ is ‘of these were leading’, but ἦρχ’ is elided and could stand for the singular ἦρχε or the plural ἦρχον; the English takes the plural, the two sons leading together, and υἷες Ἄρηος is ‘sons of Ares’ (Ἄρηος the epic genitive). οὓς τέκεν Ἀστυόχη: τέκεν is the unaugmented aorist ‘bore’. δόμῳ Ἄκτορος Ἀζεΐδαο is ‘in the house of Actor, son of Azeus’, Ἀζεΐδαο a patronymic with the epic genitive -αο. The sentence goes on into the next lines.

sentences.t:
παρθένος αἰδοίη ὑπερώϊον εἰσαναβᾶσα
Ἄρηϊ κρατερῷ·
sentences.tr:
parthenos aidoiē hyperōïon eisanabasa
Arēï kraterōi·
sentences.l:
a maiden, revered, to the upper room having gone up,
to strong Ares;
sentences.i: a revered maiden, when she had gone up to the upper room to strong Ares;
sentences.n: The story of how the two were fathered. παρθένος αἰδοίη is ‘a revered maiden’ (αἰδοῖος ‘revered’), ὑπερώϊον ‘the upper room’, and εἰσαναβᾶσα the aorist participle of εἰσαναβαίνω ‘go up into’. Ἄρηϊ κρατερῷ is a dative, ‘to strong Ares’: the sense is that she went up to be with him. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 515.

sentences.t: ὃ δέ οἱ παρελέξατο λάθρῃ·
sentences.tr: ho de hoi parelexato lathrēi·
sentences.l: and he lay beside her in secret;
sentences.i: and he lay with her in secret;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is ‘and he’, Ares, and οἱ is the enclitic dative ‘to her’. παρελέξατο is the aorist middle of παραλέγομαι ‘lie beside’, here ‘lie with’. λάθρῃ is ‘in secret’. The unit is short because it lies between two ano teleiai in the same line.

sentences.t: τοῖς δὲ τριήκοντα γλαφυραὶ νέες ἐστιχόωντο.
sentences.tr: tois de triēkonta glaphyrai nees estichoōnto.
sentences.l: and for them thirty hollow ships went in line.
sentences.i: and thirty hollow ships went in line with them.
sentences.n: The ships of this entry. τοῖς is ‘for them, with them’, and τριήκοντα ‘thirty’ is the number. γλαφυραί ‘hollow’ is the epithet of ships, as in νηυσὶ γλαφυρῇσι at 2.454. ἐστιχόωντο is the imperfect of στιχάομαι ‘go in line’, with the epic stretched -όω-; the other entries of this stretch have κίον or ἕποντο.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Φωκήων Σχεδίος καὶ Ἐπίστροφος ἦρχον
υἷες Ἰφίτου μεγαθύμου Ναυβολίδαο,
sentences.tr:
autar Phōkēōn Schedios kai Epistrophos ērchon
huies Iphitou megathymou Naubolidao,
sentences.l:
But of the Phocians Schedius and Epistrophus were leading,
sons of great-hearted Iphitus, Naubolus’-son,
sentences.i: Schedius and Epistrophus led the Phocians, sons of great-hearted Iphitus, the son of Naubolus,
sentences.n: The Phocians. αὐτάρ ‘but’ begins the entry, and Φωκήων is the genitive plural of Φωκεύς. The leaders are Σχεδίος and Ἐπίστροφος, with υἷες ‘sons’ in apposition. Ἰφίτου μεγαθύμου Ναυβολίδαο is ‘of great-hearted Iphitus, Naubolus’ son’: Ναυβολίδαο is a patronymic with the epic genitive -αο, and μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’ is the stock epithet. ἦρχον is ‘were leading’, as at 494.

sentences.t:
οἳ Κυπάρισσον ἔχον Πυθῶνά τε πετρήεσσαν
Κρῖσάν τε ζαθέην καὶ Δαυλίδα καὶ Πανοπῆα,
sentences.tr:
hoi Kyparisson echon Pythōna te petrēessan
Krisan te zatheēn kai Daulida kai Panopēa,
sentences.l:
who held Cyparissus, and rocky Pytho,
and most holy Crisa, and Daulis, and Panopeus,
sentences.i: who held Cyparissus and rocky Pytho, most holy Crisa, Daulis and Panopeus,
sentences.n: Places as accusatives after ἔχον ‘held’: Κυπάρισσον, Πυθῶνα (Pytho, the old name of the place later called Delphi), Κρῖσαν, Δαυλίδα and Πανοπῆα, the accusative of Πανοπεύς. The epithets are the ones already seen: πετρήεσσαν ‘rocky’ and ζαθέην ‘most holy’.

sentences.t:
οἵ τ’ Ἀνεμώρειαν καὶ Ὑάμπολιν ἀμφενέμοντο,
οἵ τ’ ἄρα πὰρ ποταμὸν Κηφισὸν δῖον ἔναιον,
οἵ τε Λίλαιαν ἔχον πηγῇς ἔπι Κηφισοῖο·
sentences.tr:
hoi t’ Anemōreian kai Hyampolin amphenemonto,
hoi t’ ara par potamon Kēphison dion enaion,
hoi te Lilaian echon pēgēis epi Kēphisoio·
sentences.i: and those who inhabited the country around Anemoreia and Hyampolis, those who dwelt beside the heavenly river Cephisus, and those who held Lilaea at the springs of the Cephisus;
sentences.n: Three more clauses. ἀμφενέμοντο is the imperfect middle of ἀμφινέμομαι ‘inhabit around’. ἔναιον is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’ (ἄρα, a weak ‘then’, is left untranslated); πὰρ is παρά, and ποταμὸν Κηφισὸν δῖον is ‘the river Cephisus, heavenly’, δῖον being the stock epithet ‘heavenly’, here of a river. Λίλαιαν ἔχον is ‘held Lilaea’, and πηγῇς ἔπι Κηφισοῖο is ‘at the springs of the Cephisus’: ἔπι stands after its noun, πηγῇς is the dative plural of πηγή, and Κηφισοῖο is the epic genitive. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τοῖς δ’ ἅμα τεσσαράκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.tr: tois d’ hama tessarakonta melainai nēes heponto.
sentences.l: And with them forty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with them forty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The formula that closes an entry, with the number changing: τοῖς δ’ ἅμα … μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο, ‘and with them … black ships followed’. ἅμα ‘together with’ takes the dative τοῖς; τεσσαράκοντα is ‘forty’; μέλαιναι is the feminine plural of μέλας ‘black’, the stock epithet of ships; and ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, unaugmented. The same line with τῷ for τοῖς ends the entries of the Locrians (534) and the Abantes (545).

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν Φωκήων στίχας ἵστασαν ἀμφιέποντες,
Βοιωτῶν δ’ ἔμπλην ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ θωρήσσοντο.
sentences.tr:
hoi men Phōkēōn stichas histasan amphiepontes,
Boiōtōn d’ emplēn ep’ aristera thōrēssonto.
sentences.l:
These the ranks of the Phocians were setting up, busying themselves about them,
and next to the Boeotians, on the left, were arming themselves.
sentences.i: These drew up the ranks of the Phocians, busying themselves about them, and were arming themselves on the left, next to the Boeotians.
sentences.n: οἳ μέν … δέ is ‘these … and …’, the people of the entry just ended, not named again; the Greek does not say whether the first verb has only the two leaders as subject or the whole contingent, and the English leaves it open. ἵστασαν is the imperfect third plural of ἵστημι in its transitive sense, ‘set up, draw up’, and στίχας is ‘ranks’; ἀμφιέποντες is the participle of ἀμφιέπω ‘busy oneself about’. ἔμπλην is ‘close beside’ and takes the genitive Βοιωτῶν; ἐπ’ ἀριστερά is ‘on the left’; and θωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, so ‘were arming themselves’.

sentences.t:
Λοκρῶν δ’ ἡγεμόνευεν Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας
μείων, οὔ τι τόσος γε ὅσος Τελαμώνιος Αἴας
ἀλλὰ πολὺ μείων·
sentences.tr:
Lokrōn d’ hēgemoneuen Oïlēos tachys Aias
meiōn, ou ti tosos ge hosos Telamōnios Aias
alla poly meiōn·
sentences.i: Swift Ajax, son of Oileus, was leader of the Locrians, the smaller man, not at all so big as Telamonian Ajax, but much smaller;
sentences.n: Two heroes are called Ajax, and this entry tells them apart. This one is the son of Oileus (Ὀϊλῆος, the genitive of Ὀϊλεύς), and Τελαμώνιος Αἴας ‘Telamonian Ajax’, the son of Telamon, is the other, one of ‘the two Ajaxes’ of 2.406. ἡγεμόνευεν is ‘was leader’, with the genitive Λοκρῶν ‘of the Locrians’, and ταχύς ‘swift’ is the stock epithet. μείων is the comparative ‘smaller’; οὔ τι τόσος γε ὅσος is ‘not at all so big as’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 529.

sentences.t:
ὀλίγος μὲν ἔην λινοθώρηξ,
ἐγχείῃ δ’ ἐκέκαστο Πανέλληνας καὶ Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr:
oligos men eēn linothōrēx,
encheiēi d’ ekekasto Panellēnas kai Achaious·
sentences.l:
little he was, linen-breastplated,
but with the spear he excelled the Hellenes all together and the Achaeans;
sentences.i: he was small, and wore a linen breastplate, but with the spear he excelled all the Hellenes and Achaeans;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 529. ὀλίγος is ‘small’ (ἔην = ἦν). λινοθώρηξ is a compound of λίνον ‘linen’ and θώρηξ ‘breastplate’, a corselet of linen, which is the usual explanation. ἐγχείῃ, the dative of ἐγχείη ‘spear’, says with what he excelled. ἐκέκαστο is the pluperfect of καίνυμαι, used as a simple past, ‘excelled’, and takes the accusative of those surpassed, Πανέλληνας καὶ Ἀχαιούς, ‘the Hellenes all together and the Achaeans’; Πανέλληνας is built like Παναχαιῶν at 2.404, ‘of the Achaeans all together’.

sentences.t:
οἳ Κῦνόν τ’ ἐνέμοντ’ Ὀπόεντά τε Καλλίαρόν τε
Βῆσσάν τε Σκάρφην τε καὶ Αὐγειὰς ἐρατεινὰς
Τάρφην τε Θρόνιον τε Βοαγρίου ἀμφὶ ῥέεθρα·
sentences.tr:
hoi Kynon t’ enemont’ Opoenta te Kalliaron te
Bēssan te Skarphēn te kai Augeias erateinas
Tarphēn te Thronion te Boagriou amphi rheethra·
sentences.i: who inhabited Cynus, Opoeis and Calliarus, Bessa, Scarphe and lovely Augeiae, Tarphe and Thronium, around the streams of the Boagrius;
sentences.n: The Locrians’ towns. ἐνέμοντ’ (ἐνέμοντο) is ‘inhabited’, with the accusatives Κῦνον, Ὀπόεντα (Opoeis, the place later called Opus), Καλλίαρον, Βῆσσαν, Σκάρφην, Αὐγειάς (a plural name), Τάρφην and Θρόνιον. ἐρατεινάς is ‘lovely’. Βοαγρίου ἀμφὶ ῥέεθρα is ‘around the streams of the Boagrius’, a river; ῥέεθρα is the epic plural of ῥέεθρον ‘stream’, as at 2.461.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἅμα τεσσαράκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο
Λοκρῶν, οἳ ναίουσι πέρην ἱερῆς Εὐβοίης.
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ hama tessarakonta melainai nēes heponto
Lokrōn, hoi naiousi perēn hierēs Euboiēs.
sentences.l:
And with him forty black ships followed
of the Locrians, who dwell across from sacred Euboea.
sentences.i: And with him forty black ships followed, of the Locrians, who dwell across from sacred Euboea.
sentences.n: The entry’s closing line is the formula of 524, with τῷ ‘with him’ (Ajax) for τοῖς, and here it runs on: Λοκρῶν ‘of the Locrians’ says whose the ships are, and a relative clause follows. ναίουσι is ‘dwell’, and πέρην is ‘across, on the far side of’ with the genitive ἱερῆς Εὐβοίης ‘sacred Euboea’ (ἱερός ‘sacred’, with the Ionic genitive -ῆς). The Locrians’ land faces the island across the strait.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ Εὔβοιαν ἔχον μένεα πνείοντες Ἄβαντες
Χαλκίδα τ’ Εἰρέτριάν τε πολυστάφυλόν θ’ Ἱστίαιαν
Κήρινθόν τ’ ἔφαλον Δίου τ’ αἰπὺ πτολίεθρον,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ Euboian echon menea pneiontes Abantes
Chalkida t’ Eiretrian te polystaphylon th’ Histiaian
Kērinthon t’ ephalon Diou t’ aipy ptoliethron,
sentences.l:
And those who held Euboea, breathing might, the Abantes,
and Chalcis and Eretria and Histiaea rich in grapes,
and Cerinthus by the sea and Dium’s steep citadel,
sentences.i: The Abantes, breathing might, held Euboea, and Chalcis and Eretria and Histiaea, rich in grapes, and Cerinthus by the sea and the steep citadel of Dium,
sentences.n: The Abantes of Euboea. οἳ δ’ … ἔχον ‘and those who held’ takes Εὔβοιαν, Χαλκίδα, Εἰρέτριαν, Ἱστίαιαν, Κήρινθον and the citadel of Dium, and Ἄβαντες is in apposition to οἵ. μένεα πνείοντες is ‘breathing might’: μένος is ‘might’ (the plural μένεα, as often), and πνείοντες is the participle of πνέω ‘breathe’. πολυστάφυλον is ‘rich in grapes’ (πολύ- ‘many’ + σταφυλή ‘grape-cluster’), ἔφαλον ‘by the sea’ (ἔφαλος ‘on the sea’), and Δίου τ’ αἰπὺ πτολίεθρον ‘and Dium’s steep citadel’, αἰπύς being ‘steep’.

sentences.t:
οἵ τε Κάρυστον ἔχον ἠδ’ οἳ Στύρα ναιετάασκον,
τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευ’ Ἐλεφήνωρ ὄζος Ἄρηος
Χαλκωδοντιάδης μεγαθύμων ἀρχὸς Ἀβάντων.
sentences.tr:
hoi te Karyston echon ēd’ hoi Styra naietaaskon,
tōn auth’ hēgemoneu’ Elephēnōr ozos Arēos
Chalkōdontiadēs megathymōn archos Abantōn.
sentences.l:
and who held Carystus, and who Styra kept dwelling in,
of these again was leader Elephenor, scion of Ares,
Chalcodon’s son, commander of the great-hearted Abantes.
sentences.i: and those who held Carystus and those who dwelt in Styra; of these, in turn, Elephenor, scion of Ares, the son of Chalcodon, commander of the great-hearted Abantes, was the leader.
sentences.n: οἵ τε Κάρυστον ἔχον is ‘and who held Carystus’, and ἠδ’ οἳ Στύρα ναιετάασκον is ‘and who dwelt in Styra’, ναιετάασκον being the iterative imperfect of ναιετάω (the suffix -ασκ- gives ‘kept dwelling’) and Στύρα a neuter plural. τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευ’ … is the formula ‘of these again was leader …’, which recurs at 552 and 563 (ἡγεμόνευ’ is elided ἡγεμόνευε; αὖθ’ is αὖθι, a by-form of αὖθις and αὖτε, ‘again, in turn’). ὄζος, literally ‘branch’, is ‘scion’, and Ἄρηος is the epic genitive of Ἄρης. Χαλκωδοντιάδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Chalcodon’. ἀρχός is ‘commander’, and μεγαθύμων ‘great-hearted’ is the stock epithet, here of the Abantes.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἅμ’ Ἄβαντες ἕποντο θοοὶ ὄπιθεν κομόωντες
αἰχμηταὶ μεμαῶτες ὀρεκτῇσιν μελίῃσι
θώρηκας ῥήξειν δηΐων ἀμφὶ στήθεσσι·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ham’ Abantes heponto thooi opithen komoōntes
aichmētai memaōtes orektēisin meliēisi
thōrēkas rhēxein dēïōn amphi stēthessi·
sentences.i: With him followed the Abantes, swift spearmen who wore their hair long behind, eager to break the breastplates about their enemies’ chests with outstretched ash-spears;
sentences.n: The Abantes themselves. τῷ δ’ ἅμ’ is ‘and with him’; θοοί ‘swift’ is a stock epithet, and ὄπιθεν κομόωντες is ‘wearing the hair long behind’ (κομάω ‘wear long hair’, which is also the verb of κάρη κομόωντες). αἰχμηταί are ‘spearmen’. μεμαῶτες is ‘eager’; the instrumental dative ὀρεκτῇσιν μελίῃσι, ‘with outstretched ash-spears’, belongs to ῥήξειν, and the English moves it to the end (ὀρεκτός, from ὀρέγω ‘stretch out’, and μελίη, the ash-spear of the Odyssey). ῥήξειν is the future infinitive of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, θώρηκας ‘breastplates’, δηΐων the genitive plural of δήϊος ‘hostile’, used as a noun, ‘of enemies’, and ἀμφὶ στήθεσσι ‘about the chests’.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἅμα τεσσαράκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ hama tessarakonta melainai nēes heponto.
sentences.l: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula again, as at 524 and in the first half of 534, with τῷ ‘with him’, Elephenor. The ships are black (μέλαιναι) and forty (τεσσαράκοντα), and ἕποντο is ‘followed’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἀθήνας εἶχον ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον
δῆμον Ἐρεχθῆος μεγαλήτορος, ὅν ποτ’ Ἀθήνη
θρέψε Διὸς θυγάτηρ, τέκε δὲ ζείδωρος ἄρουρα,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ar’ Athēnas eichon eÿktimenon ptoliethron
dēmon Erechthēos megalētoros, hon pot’ Athēnē
threpse Dios thygatēr, teke de zeidōros aroura,
sentences.l:
And those who held Athens, the well-built citadel,
the land of great-spirited Erechtheus, whom once Athena
reared, the daughter of Zeus, and the grain-giving plough-land bore him,
sentences.i: And those who held Athens, the well-built citadel, the land of great-spirited Erechtheus, whom Athena, the daughter of Zeus, once reared, and the grain-giving plough-land bore him,
sentences.n: Athens. οἳ δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and those who’, with ἄρ’ marking the sequence, and Ἀθήνας is the accusative plural ‘Athens’, distinct from Ἀθήνη ‘Athena’. ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον, ‘the well-built citadel’, stands in apposition with δῆμον Ἐρεχθῆος, ‘the land of Erechtheus’; δῆμος is ‘land’, the place, and μεγαλήτορος is ‘great-spirited’. ὅν is the relative ‘whom’. θρέψε is the unaugmented aorist of τρέφω ‘rear’. ζείδωρος ἄρουρα ‘the grain-giving plough-land’ is the Odyssey’s phrase (3.3), where an ancient alternative reading takes the first part as ‘life’ (from ζάω), ‘life-giving’; the plough-land is the earth, which bore him, while Athena reared him.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δ’ ἐν Ἀθήνῃς εἷσεν ἑῷ ἐν πίονι νηῷ·
ἔνθα δέ μιν ταύροισι καὶ ἀρνειοῖς ἱλάονται
κοῦροι Ἀθηναίων περιτελλομένων ἐνιαυτῶν·
sentences.tr:
kad d’ en Athēnēis heisen heōi en pioni nēōi·
entha de min tauroisi kai arneiois hilaontai
kouroi Athēnaiōn peritellomenōn eniautōn·
sentences.i: and set him down in Athens, in her own rich temple; and there the young men of the Athenians appease him with bulls and rams as the years come round;
sentences.n: κὰδ is κατά with the final vowel dropped, and εἷσεν, the aorist of ἵζω ‘set’, is separated from it (tmesis): ‘set down’. ἑῷ is the possessive ‘her own’, not the relative; πίονι is the dative of πίων ‘rich, fat’, and νηῷ the dative of νηός ‘temple’. In ἔνθα δέ μιν … ἱλάονται the subject is κοῦροι Ἀθηναίων ‘the young men of the Athenians’, μιν is Erechtheus, and ταύροισι καὶ ἀρνειοῖς are ‘bulls and rams’. ἱλάονται is the epic present middle of ἱλάομαι, the same verb as ἱλάσκομαι ‘appease’. περιτελλομένων ἐνιαυτῶν is a genitive absolute, ‘as the years come round’, so the sacrifice is repeated every year.

sentences.t: τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευ’ υἱὸς Πετεῶο Μενεσθεύς.
sentences.tr: tōn auth’ hēgemoneu’ huios Peteōo Menestheus.
sentences.l: Of these again was leader the son of Peteos, Menestheus.
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, Menestheus, the son of Peteos, was the leader.
sentences.n: The leader formula of 540, here with Μενεσθεύς, whose father’s name is the genitive Πετεῶο (of Πετεώς, in the epic ending -ο). υἱὸς Πετεῶο is ‘the son of Peteos’, set before the name as a title.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ οὔ πώ τις ὁμοῖος ἐπιχθόνιος γένετ’ ἀνὴρ
κοσμῆσαι ἵππους τε καὶ ἀνέρας ἀσπιδιώτας·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ou pō tis homoios epichthonios genet’ anēr
kosmēsai hippous te kai aneras aspidiōtas·
sentences.l:
And to him not yet any like, a man upon the earth, was born
at setting in order horses and shield-bearing men;
sentences.i: No man on earth had yet been born his equal in marshalling horses and shield-bearing men;
sentences.n: A claim about Menestheus’ skill. τῷ is ‘to him’ and goes with ὁμοῖος ‘like, equal’: no one was his equal. ἐπιχθόνιος ἀνήρ is ‘a man upon the earth’ (ἐπιχθόνιος ‘earthly’), and γένετ’ is the unaugmented aorist of γίγνομαι, ‘was born’. The infinitive κοσμῆσαι ‘to set in order’, the verb of διεκόσμεον (476), says in what. ἀσπιδιώτας is ‘shield-bearing’, formed from ἀσπίς ‘shield’.

sentences.t: Νέστωρ οἶος ἔριζεν·
sentences.tr: Nestōr oios erizen·
sentences.l: Nestor alone rivalled (him);
sentences.i: Only Nestor rivalled him;
sentences.n: ἔριζεν is the imperfect of ἐρίζω, ‘rival’; the Greek has no object, and the English supplies ‘him’, Menestheus. The word is used of contending in skill, not of quarrelling. οἶος is ‘alone’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 555.

sentences.t: ὃ γὰρ προγενέστερος ἦεν·
sentences.tr: ho gar progenesteros ēen·
sentences.l: for he was older;
sentences.i: for he was older;
sentences.n: ὃ γάρ is ‘for he’, giving the reason Nestor was the one rival. προγενέστερος is the comparative of προγενής ‘born before’, so ‘older’, and ἦεν is the epic form of ἦν.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἅμα πεντήκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.tr: tōi d’ hama pentēkonta melainai nēes heponto.
sentences.l: And with him fifty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with him fifty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula of an entry, as at 524, here for the Athenians: τῷ δ’ ἅμα ‘and with him’ (Menestheus), πεντήκοντα ‘fifty’, μέλαιναι νῆες ‘black ships’, and ἕποντο ‘followed’, the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ ἐκ Σαλαμῖνος ἄγεν δυοκαίδεκα νῆας,
στῆσε δ’ ἄγων ἵν’ Ἀθηναίων ἵσταντο φάλαγγες.
sentences.tr:
Aias d’ ek Salaminos agen dyokaideka nēas,
stēse d’ agōn hin’ Athēnaiōn histanto phalanges.
sentences.l:
And Ajax from Salamis brought twelve ships,
and, bringing them, stationed them where the Athenians’ battle-lines were taking their stand.
sentences.i: And Ajax brought twelve ships from Salamis, and led them up and stationed them where the Athenians’ battle-lines stood.
sentences.n: Ajax of Salamis. The poet says only Αἴας and names his island, Σαλαμῖνος; the reader knows from 528 that this is the Telamonian Ajax, the greater. ἄγεν is the unaugmented ἦγεν, and δυοκαίδεκα is ‘twelve’. στῆσε is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι in its transitive sense; the English supplies ‘them’, the ships, as its object. ἄγων is the participle ‘leading’. ἵν’ is ‘where’, and Ἀθηναίων ἵσταντο φάλαγγες is ‘the battle-lines of the Athenians were taking their stand’, φάλαγγες being ‘lines of battle’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ Ἄργός τ’ εἶχον Τίρυνθά τε τειχιόεσσαν
Ἑρμιόνην Ἀσίνην τε, βαθὺν κατὰ κόλπον ἐχούσας,
Τροιζῆν’ Ἠϊόνας τε καὶ ἀμπελόεντ’ Ἐπίδαυρον,
οἵ τ’ ἔχον Αἴγιναν Μάσητά τε κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ Argos t’ eichon Tiryntha te teichioessan
Hermionēn Asinēn te, bathyn kata kolpon echousas,
Troizēn’ Ēïonas te kai ampeloent’ Epidauron,
hoi t’ echon Aiginan Masēta te kouroi Achaiōn,
sentences.l:
And those who held Argos and walled Tiryns,
Hermione and Asine, which hold a deep gulf,
Troezen and Eïones and vine-clad Epidaurus,
and who held Aegina and Mases, young men of the Achaeans,
sentences.i: And those who held Argos and walled Tiryns, Hermione and Asine, which hold a deep gulf, Troezen, Eïones and vine-clad Epidaurus, and the young men of the Achaeans who held Aegina and Mases,
sentences.n: The men of Argos and its neighbourhood. οἳ δ’ … εἶχον is ‘and those who held’, and Ἄργος is the city. τειχιόεσσαν is ‘walled’ (from τεῖχος ‘wall’), the epithet of Tiryns. In βαθὺν κατὰ κόλπον ἐχούσας the κατά is separated from its verb (tmesis), κατέχω ‘hold’, so ‘which hold a deep gulf’, ἐχούσας agreeing with Ἑρμιόνην and Ἀσίνην. Τροιζῆν’ is the elided Τροιζῆνα. ἀμπελόεντ’ is ἀμπελόεντα ‘vine-clad’ (from ἄμπελος ‘vine’). οἵ τ’ ἔχον is ‘and who held’, with κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν ‘the young men of the Achaeans’ as subject; Μάσητα is the accusative of Μάσης.

sentences.t:
τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης
καὶ Σθένελος, Καπανῆος ἀγακλειτοῦ φίλος υἱός·
sentences.tr:
tōn auth’ hēgemoneue boēn agathos Diomēdēs
kai Sthenelos, Kapanēos agakleitou philos huios·
sentences.l:
Of these again was leader Diomedes, good at the war-cry,
and Sthenelus, the dear son of renowned Capaneus;
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, Diomedes, good at the war-cry, was the leader, and Sthenelus, the dear son of renowned Capaneus;
sentences.n: The leader formula (540, 552), with two names: ἡγεμόνευε is singular, so Σθένελος is added to the subject as an afterthought. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is the epithet the Odyssey gives Menelaus (3.311), with βοήν an accusative of respect. Καπανῆος is the epic genitive of Καπανεύς; ἀγακλειτοῦ is ‘renowned’, as the Odyssey renders ἀγακλειτός; φίλος υἱός is ‘dear son’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἅμ’ Εὐρύαλος τρίτατος κίεν ἰσόθεος φὼς
Μηκιστέος υἱὸς Ταλαϊονίδαο ἄνακτος·
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ ham’ Euryalos tritatos kien isotheos phōs
Mēkisteos huios Talaïonidao anaktos·
sentences.l:
And with them Euryalus, as third, went, a man equal to a god,
son of Mecisteus, Talaion’s-son, the lord;
sentences.i: And with them went Euryalus as the third, a man the equal of a god, the son of lord Mecisteus, Talaion’s son;
sentences.n: A third leader. τοῖσι δ’ ἅμ’ … κίεν is ‘and with them went’, κίεν being the imperfect of κίω ‘go’. Εὐρύαλος is Euryalus, and τρίτατος ‘as third’ is a form of τρίτος, he being the third of the three leaders. ἰσόθεος φώς is ‘a man equal to a god’, the Odyssey’s phrase, φώς meaning ‘man’. Μηκιστέος is the genitive of Μηκιστεύς, and Ταλαϊονίδαο ἄνακτος, ‘Talaion’s son, the lord’, describes Mecisteus: Ταλαϊονίδαο is a patronymic with the epic genitive -αο.

sentences.t: συμπάντων δ’ ἡγεῖτο βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: sympantōn d’ hēgeito boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: And of all together was leading Diomedes, good at the war-cry;
sentences.i: and Diomedes, good at the war-cry, led them all;
sentences.n: Diomedes has the supreme command. συμπάντων, from σύν and πάντες, is ‘of all together’, and ἡγεῖτο is the imperfect middle of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’, which takes the genitive. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is the same epithet as at 563.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δ’ ἅμ’ ὀγδώκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.tr: toisi d’ ham’ ogdōkonta melainai nēes heponto.
sentences.l: And with them eighty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with them eighty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula of an entry, as at 524, here for the whole Argive force: τοῖσι δ’ ἅμ’ ‘and with them’, ὀγδώκοντα ‘eighty’, the largest number so far in this stretch, μέλαιναι νῆες ‘black ships’, and ἕποντο ‘followed’.
